Iran Warns of 'More Painful' Retaliation After US Strikes Three Oil Tankers in Gulf, Raising Fears of Wider Escalation
Tehran says the 'era of proportionate responses' is over as attacks at sea heighten scrutiny of commercial shipping near the Strait of Hormuz
Iran's threat of a 'faster, heavier and more painful' retaliation came after US forces said they struck three Iranian oil tankers in the Gulf of Oman, permanently disabling two and destroying a third, in one of the most serious recent confrontations between Washington and Tehran at sea.
Iran has declared the era of 'proportionate responses' over, with parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf warning that any further attack on the country's interests or security would draw a 'faster, heavier and more painful' response.
Ghalibaf's remarks followed US strikes on three Iranian crude oil carriers after the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, or IRGC, launched ballistic missiles towards two US Navy warships patrolling regional waters, according to US Central Command (CENTCOM).
The command said the vessels successfully evaded the missile attacks and that no American personnel were harmed.
US Says Three Iranian Tankers Struck
US Central Command said American forces permanently disabled two Iranian crude oil carriers and destroyed a third, which it said later sank in the Gulf of Oman.
CENTCOM identified the vessels as the M/T Downy, off the coast of Kharg Island; the M/T Stark 1, near Jask; and the M/T Kylo, also known as the Noxen. The command said the Kylo was unladen and that its crew had been ordered to abandon ship before US forces struck it at several critical points, rendering it inoperable.
The US military said the operation was a response to what it described as failed Iranian missile attacks on an aircraft carrier and a guided‑missile destroyer. CENTCOM alleged that the targeted tankers were linked to a multibillion‑dollar network that finances the IRGC and its regional proxy forces. Iran has not accepted that characterisation.
Admiral Brad Cooper, commander of US Central Command, said Washington would impose 'an even higher economic cost' if Iranian forces fired on US naval vessels.
'Let the message to the IRGC be clear: If you shoot at two of our ships, we will impose an even higher economic cost — taking out three of yours,' Cooper said. 'We will not hesitate to defend American forces and, if necessary, destroy Iran's limited and exposed oil fleet.'
Tehran Signals Tougher Retaliation
In a statement posted on Telegram and carried by Iranian media, Ghalibaf said the US should understand 'before it is too late' that 'the rules of the game have changed'.
'Any aggression against Iran's interests and security will receive a faster, heavier and more painful response,' he said. Iran later said its naval forces had targeted three oil tankers that it accused of travelling through the Strait of Hormuz via an 'unauthorised route'.
The IRGC also said it had struck three US‑linked vessels in other areas and warned shipping not to use routes it had not approved. Those assertions have not been independently verified, and the US account of the confrontation differs from Tehran's.
Iranian state media further claimed that Iranian naval forces had attacked an American military unmanned surface vessel attempting to enter the Strait of Hormuz.
CENTCOM has disputed Iranian accounts of the wider maritime confrontation, saying its warships evaded the missile attacks, and a CENTCOM spokesman called the USV claim 'a total lie.' No independent confirmation of Iran's unmanned‑vessel claim was immediately available.
Global Oil Chokepoint Under Strain
The latest exchange has heightened concern over security in and around the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow waterway linking the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and a key route for global energy shipments.
Even limited attacks on tankers, port infrastructure or naval patrols can disrupt commercial routing, raise insurance and freight costs, and increase pressure on oil markets.
The risk is not confined to ships directly involved in the confrontation: commercial crews, insurers and regional authorities must weigh the possibility of misidentification, sea mines, missile launches or further restrictions on transit.
The confrontation follows a renewed phase of US‑Iranian military exchanges in recent days. CENTCOM has said earlier US operations targeted IRGC air‑defence sites, radar systems, maritime assets, mine‑laying capabilities and communications facilities, following what it described as attempted Iranian attacks on commercial shipping and US personnel.
For now, the competing statements leave questions unresolved, including the full extent of damage to the vessels, the status of the ships Iran said it targeted, and whether either side will take further action in one of the world's most strategically sensitive waterways.

(DCNF)—Secretary of Energy Chris Wright outlined America’s long-term goal for securing global trade passing through the Strait of Hormuz even as its conflict with Iran threatens such traffic.
Wright touted the sustained traffic transiting the Strait of Hormuz before telling Dana Bash during a “State of the Union” interview Sunday that securing the passageway “shouldn’t be just the United States’s responsibility” looking forward. His appearance on the CNN show comes the day after U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) forces reported taking out three Iranian oil tankers.
“The president says the Strait of Hormuz is under U.S. control. Just yesterday, the U.S. struck three Iranian tankers in retaliation for Iran firing missiles at U.S. warships. Meanwhile, The New York Times reports that Iran struck at least 23 merchant ships in the Strait in the last two months,” Bash said before asking Wright, “Does that sound to you like it’s a situation completely under control?”
“Our transits through the Strait are averaging over 9 million barrels a day now. And with the access pipelines that go around the Strait, we’re probably two-thirds or more of pre-conflict flows,” Wright responded. “So Iranians are still causing trouble, but the United States Navy is winning that battle.”
Bash then asked Wright if he is suggesting that the U.S. Navy is going to have to stay in the Strait “indefinitely” to maintain the current flow of oil and tankers.
“Oh, I think we’ll see a change in the Iranian regime, or certainly a change in their policy if they want to become a trading nation again and engage with the world,” Wright said. “But they have not lightly given up their nuclear weapons program.”
In parallel with military operations, the U.S. Department of the Treasury launched Operation Economic Outcast on Aug. 24 to sanction those who trade with Iran.
“Thank God for President Trump‘s courage to take this on,” Wright continued. “He did not want to kick the can down to the road to the next administration to deal with a nuclear-armed Iran. This is Iran without nuclear weapons; imagine Iran with nuclear weapons.”
Bash then doubled down, asking if the U.S. Navy being in the Strait is “just the new normal now?”
“Well, it is today, but I think, as you look forward, other nations will come and work with us in this endeavor,” Wright responded. “Certainly, trade for the world is important. It shouldn’t be just the United States’ responsibility. But until Iran changes their position or changes their government, we’ll have to deal with them. But, slowly, their capabilities are being degraded and ours are being enhanced.”
Bash then told Wright that “what’s unsaid in this discussion so far is that it’s just— it’s not safe.”
“The New York Times also says August was the deadliest month for merchants in the Strait of Hormuz since March,” she continued before asking Wright if he can “unequivocally say that ships that want to transit through the Strait of Hormuz can do so safely?”
“We‘re working cooperatively with fleets that do want to transit,” Wright said. “Some ships aren’t transiting, and, of course, that’s their choice, but the United States is working with teams from all the nations in the Gulf to get transits and to continue to ramp them up. Iranian ships, of course, are not transiting at all. That’s a ticking time bomb for the economy of Iran.”
“But look, we’re trying to end a 47-year conflict as Iran dashes to develop nuclear weapons and wreak havoc on their neighbors and threaten the world economy,” he later added. “Is there some effort involved in that? Why, of course.”

The U.S. military struck three Iranian crude oil tankers on September 5 after Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps fired ballistic missiles toward two U.S. Navy warships in regional waters.
CNN reported that U.S. Central Command said an American aircraft carrier and a guided-missile destroyer avoided the Iranian attacks, with no U.S. personnel injured. The military said two Iranian tankers were disabled near Kharg Island and Jask, while a third vessel was destroyed in the Gulf of Oman.
According to U.S. Central Command, the tankers were part of an oil network that helps finance the Revolutionary Guard and its regional partners. Iranian media had earlier reported that a tanker near Kharg Island was struck and that its crew was evacuated.
Kharg Island is a major center for Iranian crude exports, while the nearby Strait of Hormuz remains a critical route for global energy shipments. The latest exchange adds to renewed military tensions between Washington and Tehran and increases concerns about maritime security in the region.
